title: On Taiwan, US ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Is Not Dead Yet
gist: Denny Roy pushes back on claims (Crabtree in Foreign Policy, Shahn Louis, Michael Schiffer) that the Trump administration has killed U.S. 'strategic ambiguity' on Taiwan, arguing the policy still functions.

insights.claim: Under strategic ambiguity the U.S. refuses to say in advance whether it would send forces to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack.
insights.speaker: Denny Roy
insights.so_what: Baseline for interpreting any shift in U.S. Taiwan signaling that would move cross-strait risk.

insights.claim: Several analysts argue the Trump administration has made strategic ambiguity ineffective by creating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene; James Crabtree wrote on September 14 in Foreign Policy that the U.S. is 'inching more toward a position of nonintervention.'
insights.speaker: Denny Roy
insights.so_what: A perceived drift to nonintervention would raise the risk premium on Taiwan-exposed assets such as semiconductors.
insights.quote: the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.”

insights.claim: Denny Roy contends, against the prevailing commentary, that U.S. strategic ambiguity on Taiwan is not dead yet.
insights.speaker: Denny Roy
insights.so_what: If ambiguity still deters, markets may be overpricing a shift in U.S. Taiwan commitment.
